shortDescription: Polycarp was bishop of the church in Smyrna and wrote a letter to the church at Philippi. As an old man he was put to death at Smyrna, after telling the governor he had served Christ for eighty-six years.

timeline.headline: Bishop of Smyrna, and a friend of Ignatius

lines.text: Made bishop of the church in Smyrna, by apostles in Asia, Irenaeus says.
lines.note: Who made him bishop is told differently: Tertullian says the Smyrna church's records name John, and Jerome that John ordained him.

lines.text: Ignatius of Antioch, a prisoner on his way to Rome, writes from Smyrna, sending love to Polycarp.
Ignatius writes to Polycarp from Troas: he has seen his blameless face, and asks him to call a council and send a messenger to Syria, and to write to the nearby churches.
Polycarp and the presbyters with him write to the church at Philippi, which had invited him to write about righteousness.
lines.reference: Polycarp, Epistle to the Philippians, opening and 3

lines.text: The letter warns against those who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh or say there is no resurrection or judgment, and calls its readers back to the word handed down from the beginning.
He grieves over Valens, once a presbyter at Philippi.
lines.note: This chapter survives only in a Latin version.

lines.text: He sends the Philippians the letters of Ignatius written to him and his church, and all the others he has, and promises to carry their letter to Syria if he finds an opportunity.

timeline.when: In the time of Anicetus, bishop of Rome
timeline.headline: A visit to Rome, and a boy who listened
timeline.witness: Irenaeus of Lyon, who heard him as a boy

lines.text: In Lower Asia, the boy Irenaeus hears him teach, and later can still describe the place where he sat, and how he spoke of John and the others who had seen the Lord.

At Rome, he and Anicetus cannot persuade each other: Polycarp keeps what he had kept with John and the other apostles, and Anicetus the customs of the presbyters before him. They share communion and part in peace.
lines.reference: Irenaeus, letter to Victor, in Eusebius, Church History V.24.16 to 17
lines.note: Irenaeus does not name the feast here; Eusebius calls it a question about the day of the paschal feast (Church History IV.14).

lines.text: At Rome he turns many away from the heretics to the church, proclaiming the one truth he had received from the apostles.
Marcion meets him and asks whether he knows him; Polycarp answers that he knows him, the first-born of Satan.
lines.note: Irenaeus does not say where they met; Jerome, writing long after, puts it at Rome.

timeline.when: Date unknown; a great Sabbath, the second day of the month Xanthicus
timeline.headline: Hunted, tried and put to death at Smyrna
timeline.witness: The church of Smyrna, in its own account of his death

lines.text: In a time of persecution, Germanicus fights the wild beasts in the stadium, and the crowd cries out against the atheists, meaning the Christians, and for Polycarp to be sought out.
Quintus, a Phrygian who had pushed himself and others to come forward, loses heart at the sight of the beasts and sacrifices; the church says it does not praise those who give themselves up.
At the wish of many, Polycarp leaves the city for a country house nearby, where he prays night and day for all people and for the churches.
He moves to another house. The searchers seize two young slaves, and one confesses under torture.

lines.when: Friday evening, the day of the preparation
lines.text: Police and horsemen find him. He could have escaped, but says that the will of God be done, has food and drink set before them, and prays for two hours.

He is brought into the city on a donkey. Herod, the Irenarch, a local officer, and his father Nicetes urge him in their carriage to say Lord Caesar and sacrifice, then throw him out, and he hurts his leg.
In the stadium the proconsul promises to free him if he will swear and revile Christ. He answers that he has served Christ eighty-six years.
Threatened with beasts and then with fire, he answers that the proconsul threatens a fire that burns for an hour.
The crowd cries that he is the teacher of Asia and the overthrower of their gods. Philip the Asiarch will not loose a lion, since the beast shows are over, so they call for him to be burned alive.
The church says the fire took the shape of an arch, like a ship's sail filled with wind, around his body.
lines.note: A wonder, in the church's own report; it names no eyewitness.

lines.text: Since the fire does not consume his body, an executioner pierces him with a dagger.

Nicetes asks the governor not to give up the body. The centurion burns it, and the church takes up his bones and lays them in a fitting place, where it hopes to gather on the birthday of his martyrdom.
The church counts him the twelfth martyred in Smyrna, those of Philadelphia included.
The church sends its account to the church at Philomelium, which had asked for it, and asks that it be sent on to the brethren farther away.
The account dates his death to the second day of the month Xanthicus, on the great Sabbath, and gives no year.
lines.reference: Martyrdom of Polycarp 21; Eusebius, Church History IV.14.10 and IV.15; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 17
lines.note: Eusebius puts the death under Verus, the Marcus Aurelius Verus who followed Antoninus Pius; Jerome in the reign of Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

lines.text: Irenaeus calls him a more steadfast witness of truth than Valentinus, Marcion and the rest of the heretics, and commends his letter to the Philippians.
Victor, bishop of Rome, tries to cut off the churches of Asia over the Easter date. Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, writing to him, names Polycarp among the great lights of Asia.
Irenaeus writes to Victor that Polycarp and Anicetus kept communion though they differed; Eusebius calls Irenaeus a peacemaker in this matter.
Tertullian says the church of Smyrna records that John placed Polycarp there.
Copyists pass on his church's account: Gaius from the copy of Irenaeus, Socrates at Corinth, and Pionius.
lines.note: A later note, not part of the church's letter.

lines.text: Eusebius copies most of the church's account into his Church History.
Jerome writes that the letter to the Philippians is still read in the meetings in Asia.

uncertain: The witnesses. Nearly all that is known comes from his one surviving letter; his church's account of his death, which speaks of the yearly gathering as still to come and so seems to have been written within a year of it; and Irenaeus, who heard him as a boy and wrote many years later. Eusebius and Jerome wrote long after and did not know him.

The eighty-six years. Polycarp says he has served Christ eighty-six years. The text does not say whether they count from his birth or from his baptism, so they do not give his age. Irenaeus says only that he lived a very long time and died a very old man. A note in the Ante-Nicene Fathers turns the figure into his age; that is a modern inference.

The date. His church's account gives a day and a month but no year. The English prints the seventh day before the Kalends of May, where Gebhardt's Greek reads March, and the English editor's notes call the translation very doubtful and the chronology obscure. Jerome dates his own book to the fourteenth year of Theodosius; that this is more than two hundred years after Polycarp, like the second century itself, comes from modern dating, not from the sources.

The trial. In the Greek the proconsul promises to free him if he will swear by the Fortune of Caesar, and then, as a second command, tells him to revile Christ; the story joins the two, because Polycarp's answer meets the second. The governor of the story is the proconsul, and Asia is the name the sources give, with no word of a Roman province. The crowd's word atheists meant people who reject the gods; it first rose after Germanicus died bravely in the stadium, with the cry that Polycarp be sought out.

The arrest. The Greek says the searchers came at once and, not finding him, seized two young slaves, but not where; the English, by its word whither, puts it at the second farm. The Greek word can mean slave boys or young servants. That they were of his household rests on the account's word for those who betrayed him.

The wonders. The flame shaped like a sail, and the body the fire could not consume, are the Smyrna church's own report, and it names no eyewitness. The English also has a dove coming from the wound; Gebhardt's Greek brackets it as doubtful and Eusebius leaves it out, so the story does not tell it. The vision of the burning pillow, the voice from heaven and the sweet smell are left out too. The account makes hostile claims about the Jews of Smyrna that no other source tells from their side. It was addressed to Philomelium, though Eusebius says Pontus, and its messenger is Marcus in the English and Marcion in Gebhardt's Greek.

The yearly gathering. The church does not say it resolved to meet. It says the Lord will let them gather where his bones lay, as far as they can, in gladness and joy. Each year is implied by the word birthday, the day of his death seen as his birth into life. The sources used here do not say whether the gathering was kept.

The apostles. That he knew John and others who had seen the Lord rests on Irenaeus, and the sources do not say which John. Who made him bishop is told differently: Irenaeus says apostles in Asia, Tertullian that the church of Smyrna's records name John, Jerome that John ordained him, and Eusebius those who had seen and heard the Lord.

The visit to Rome. No source gives how long before his death it came; Eusebius tells it first, and the modern dates in McGiffert's notes would put it only a little before. Irenaeus's words on what Polycarp kept do not name the feast, and he does not give it as the reason for the trip; Eusebius does both. Irenaeus also says the two differed a little on other things. His words that Anicetus conceded the eucharist to Polycarp may mean that Polycarp presided or only that he took part; the story leaves them out. From the visit to Victor's accession, Eusebius's own figures give about twenty-one to thirty-two years, and the modern dates in McGiffert's notes about thirty-five.

The letter. It survives, but not whole in Greek, and the Library holds no Greek of it in readable form, so its modern English follows the English translation alone. Irenaeus says he wrote other letters, to neighboring churches and to some of the brethren; only this one is held. The letter as printed leaves it unclear whether Ignatius was still alive when it was written.

The modern English of the answer follows the Greek, my king, the one who saved me, as Eusebius's translator has it, "my king who saved me", where the Ante-Nicene English prints "my King and my Saviour". Of the yearly gathering it likewise follows the Greek word birthday, where that English prints anniversary, and the athletes' word for those who have competed, where it prints finished their course.
Marcion. Irenaeus tells of the meeting but not where it happened. Jerome, writing long after, puts it at Rome, at the time of the visit to Anicetus.
The twelve martyrs. His church calls him the twelfth martyred in Smyrna, counting those of Philadelphia. Eusebius has him die with eleven from Philadelphia, which makes all the others Philadelphians.
